title: Dynamic Preference Logic of Preference Lifting
comment: dynamic preference logic; preference lifting; framing effect;
summary: In preference logic, preference is modeled as a binary relation between possible worlds. When we discuss preference relations between propositions, we also need to consider how to lift this relation between possible worlds to propositions. Here, propositions are usually represented by their extensions, that is, sets of possible worlds. There are several choices of lifting scheme: for example, one may require even the worst world in one set to be better than the best world in another, or merely require that every world in one set have some better world in the other. The framing effect in behavioral economics shows that the lifting scheme can change with the way a question is posed or with psychological factors. This paper proves that such changes cannot be reduced to changes in preferences between possible worlds. Accordingly, we treat the lifting scheme as an independent dimension of evaluation and use a hybrid language to describe switches between lifting schemes. We thereby present a language for preference logic with dynamic lifting and prove its soundness and completeness.

title: Proper Conflict-Free Coloring of Cocomparability, Co-Bipartite, and Distance-Hereditary Graphs
summary: A proper conflict-free coloring is a proper vertex coloring in which every non-isolated vertex has a neighbor whose color occurs exactly once in its open neighborhood. We prove that deciding whether $ω(G)$ colors suffice is NP-complete on connected cocomparability graphs of diameter two and independence number three. The reduction supplies a partition into three cliques, a maximum clique, an optimal ordinary coloring, and a dominating edge. Every constructed graph needs either $ω(G)$ or $ω(G)+1$ PCF colors. The result also gives NP-completeness on AT-free graphs. For the co-bipartite subclass, we give a complete matching characterization and an $O(n^6)$-time algorithm for an optimal coloring. The cocktail-party graphs are exactly the co-bipartite graphs requiring two more colors than their ordinary chromatic number; every other co-bipartite graph needs at most one additional color. The matching method extends to all graphs with independence number at most two, giving an $O(n^6\log n)$-time optimization algorithm. Finally, for distance-hereditary graphs, we decide whether $k$ colors suffice in $O(n+m+nk^{10})$ time and compute an optimal coloring in $O(n^{11}+m)$ time without fixing the palette size. The algorithm uses a binary decomposition and groups colors according to five possible behaviors at the boundary of a subgraph.

title: Computing Weighted Set Covers with Heterogeneous Stochastic Oracles: Deadline-Constrained Token Complexity
summary:
We study computation in which a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) uses AI systems, abstracted as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs), to solve Weighted Set Cover. A pilot study shows that an LLM can outperform weighted greedy. HSOs differ in capabilities, response distributions, latencies, and token costs. We study how the PTM selects HSOs to obtain, by a deadline and with a required success probability, a full cover satisfying a prescribed weight threshold, and we analyze expected token cost.
  For queries requesting full covers, assuming independent call successes and uninformative failures, we characterize by linear programming the minimum expected token cost for every feasible success probability. An optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches. Among policies attaining maximum success probability, the expected cost reduction of two-batch selection relative to querying all oracles in one batch is nonnegative and submodular. We construct an FPTAS for near-optimal cost reduction under heterogeneous response-time bounds. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm for positive integral expected token costs.
  For partial-cover responses, the PTM combines returned sets across batches and turns. Once their union covers the universe, it verifies total weight directly or obtains a guarantee from LP-dual tests on retained partial covers. We give one-turn probability, token-cost, and hardness results and adaptive token-cost bounds under per-batch assumptions. A constructed instance shows that residual-guided querying can reduce expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of possible residual subproblems.

title: BitPrefill: W1.58A4 Tensor-Core Acceleration for Compute-Bound LLM Prefill
summary: Low-bit quantization reduces large language model (LLM) inference cost, yet implementations optimized for memory-bound decode can leave compute-bound prefill on BF16 tensor cores. This gap matters for input-heavy workloads, including long-context and multimodal applications, where prefill can account for a substantial fraction of inference latency. We propose a W1.58A4 operator that quantizes weights to ternary values and activations to 4-bit, while executing the linear projection on native INT4 general matrix multiply (GEMM) tensor cores, turning prefill from a full-precision matrix multiply into a low-bit one. We deploy the operator for BitNet-b1.58 on a single RTX 4090 and a Jetson Orin Nano edge device, and report GEMM-kernel latency, end-to-end LLMs prefill latency, and task accuracy against bf16 and BitNet/BitBLAS baselines. Our proposed kernel achieves ~1.42x acceleration compared to the original BF16 prefill phase, with negligible reduction on model accuracy.

title: SDG: State-Dependent Gating at Chunk Boundaries for Linear Attention
summary: Recent gated linear attention models use state-independent gates, computed from token representations without directly reading the recurrent memory. This design supports efficient chunkwise computation: sequences are divided into chunks of consecutive tokens, with parallel computation within each chunk. However, the same token representation produces the same gate, even when the layer stores different information. We introduce State-Dependent Gating (SDG), which computes element-wise gates from the change in memory over a chunk and applies them at the chunk boundary. This provides state feedback for forgetting while preserving parallel computation within each chunk. We develop fused kernels for Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet-2, and Mamba-3. Our theoretical analysis quantifies the potential reconstruction benefits of state-dependent, element-wise gating under a signal--noise model. We also show that boundary decay is an element-wise ridge proximal step when the gate is held fixed. Empirical evaluation of 1.3B linear attention and hybrid models trained on 100B tokens shows improvements across language modeling, commonsense reasoning, synthetic and real-world retrieval, and long-context understanding. These results demonstrate that SDG is an effective approach to enhancing existing linear attention models.

title: MambaSplit: Severity-Robust and Inference-Efficient Semantic Unmixing of Fluorescence Microscopy Image Data
comment: 28 pages, 15 figures, 23 tables; main paper (8 pages) followed by supplementary material
summary: The number of structures fluorescence microscopy can image in one sample is limited by how few fluorophores can be separated without significant spectral overlap. Semantic unmixing circumvents this limit by imaging two structures in one fluorescent channel and computationally separating the superimposed image into one image per structure. Because pixels rarely identify their structure, unmixing requires both local and long-range spatial context. The relative brightness of the two structures is unknown and can be very uneven, so predictions must remain accurate across mixing severities, from balanced mixtures to ones where a structure is barely visible. Existing methods either process small image patches or add context through auxiliary pathways that slow inference on large images. We present MambaSplit, a hierarchical state-space encoder with a convolutional decoder that captures context across large tiles in linear time and predicts both channels in one deterministic pass. MambaSplit trains either on computationally summed channel images with random mixing ratios, where a lightweight head estimates the unknown ratio and conditions the decoder on it, or on experimentally acquired superpositions. Across five datasets and nine mixing ratios, MambaSplit achieves the highest RI-PSNR, by up to 3.0 dB, in 11 of 15 dataset-severity combinations and ties in one more, while running 5.9x faster than the strongest baseline. On acquired superpositions, fine-tuning a model pretrained on summed inputs matches or exceeds all baselines. Ablations show that accuracy and robustness come mainly from the training recipe: large tiles, mixing ratios sampled across their full range (up to 11 dB over fixed-ratio training), and independently drawn channel crops (3.9 dB on BioSR). The state-space backbone makes large tiles affordable, enabling high-content screening and event-driven smart microscopy.

title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
summary: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

title: A functional Breuer-Major theorem under finite variance, with application to the $R/S$ test for long memory
summary:
The Breuer-Major theorem (Breuer and Major, 1983) states that, for a function $G$ of Hermite rank $m$ such that $\mathbb{E}(G^{2}(X))<\infty$, and a stationary Gaussian sequence whose correlation function $r$ satisfies $\sum_{i}|r(i)|^{m}<\infty$, the finite dimensional distributions of the normalized partial sum process of $G(X_{i})$ converge to those of a Brownian motion. Whether the functional version of this result holds under these sole conditions has remained open for a long time, the tightness being known only under additional moment assumptions. In this paper we prove that the functional central limit theorem holds under finite variance only. More generally, we give a high order expansion of the partial sum process which covers both short and long-range dependence: the long-range dependent components converge to Hermite processes, while the remainder converges to a Brownian motion.
  As an application, we discuss the question of testing long-memory in observed data using the $R/S$ statistics. We derive the limiting distributions of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics, prove the consistency of the test and propose a data-driven choice of the truncation parameter. A Monte Carlo study compares the performances of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics for both short-memory and long-memory sequences.

title: Bird-Call Recognition Across Distance: Acoustic Degradation and BirdNET Performance
summary: As bird calls weaken with distance, their recordings lose spectral detail. We examine how species recognition varies with distance using controlled playback of ten-second excerpts from 20 bird species at seven distances from 1 to 48 ft. An STM32-based recording system acquires and stores the audio, which is subsequently analyzed on a computer using acoustic measurements and BirdNET. Across four metadata configurations, mean-aggregated top-1 accuracy is 95--100% through 24 ft, 90--95% at 36 ft, and 80--90% at 48 ft, with 20 recordings evaluated per configuration at each distance. Across the screened recordings, the median upper spectral edge is below its 1-ft reference at every evaluated distance from 4 to 36 ft, indicating an overall reduction in upper-frequency content with distance. These results show that recognition remains high through 24 ft despite measurable spectral degradation, followed by greater and configuration-dependent losses at longer distances.

title: Testing Settlement Flags after Late Evidence and Process Restart
summary: A settlement flag can survive an application restart while the economic effects remain ambiguous. We define a contract linking the fixed plan, source admission at two cutoffs, identity-keyed ledger effects and post-invocation state. We generated 504 synthetic histories, ran each through a file implementation and a separately coded SQLite implementation, and observed 672 controlled process exits. The file implementation missed 54 same-identity payment-date conflicts, including 27 that credited cash early, and a monitor using run flags, artifact presence and purchase counts accepted all 54. The same contract distinguishes a purchase awaiting closure from a correct quote wait for a single writer on a running kernel and filesystem.

title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series
summary: Functional time series have a wide range of practical applications to modeling complex datasets such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) and other biological signals. Often latent states are hidden within the data dictating how a system is behaving and changing over time. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one common and highly applicable latent state space model where the hidden state sequence evolves as a Markov chain. While the HMM has had much success modeling discrete, multivariate, and fully functional time series, it is also restricted by the Markov property which causes hidden states to persist only at geometrically decaying rates. This work investigates the implementation of hidden semi-Markov models for modeling fully functional time series data. This allows for the hidden state sequence to persist in a given state for a data-driven sojourn time, which can be parametrized by a discrete distribution (e.g. negative binomial) or left non-parametric. For efficient fitting of such a model, the hidden semi-Markov chain is embedded into a larger state space Markov chain and classic methods like the Baum-Welch and Viterbi algorithms are applied. We furthermore consider functional time series in the general setting of Gaussian measures in locally convex topological vector spaces. This is applied to a time series of pediatric EEG signals collected via overnight polysomnography.

title: Efficient Conversational Multi-Talker ASR with Predicted Speaker-Agnostic Activity Streams
summary: Multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) can be performed by conditioning a single-speaker recognizer on frame-level speaker activity. However, this approach requires a complete diarization pass to obtain the conditioning signals and one ASR pass per speaker, making both the frontend and recognition costs dependent on the number of speakers. We reduce these costs by using Heuristic Error Assignment Training (HEAT) to merge the activities of an arbitrary number of speakers into two speaker-agnostic streams. Conditioning on these streams limits recognition to two ASR passes regardless of the number of participants. Through an analysis of the resulting encoder representations, we show that under a stream-assignment heuristic suited to conversational speech, the recognizer represents a stream target much as it does a speaker target. Because the streams do not encode persistent speaker identities, we further replace the conventional sliding-window diarization and clustering frontend with a model that predicts both activity streams directly from the audio in a single pass. A combination of arrival-order and permutation-invariant training objectives over the two-stream powerset labels prevents the predictor from collapsing to identical streams. We also investigate post-hoc speaker attribution by matching decoded utterances to speaker activities within their assigned streams. Experiments on corpora with diverse conversational dynamics demonstrate a favorable efficiency--accuracy tradeoff. On AMI and ICSI, two-stream conditioning is respectively 44\% and 87\% faster than per-speaker conditioning using the same diarization frontend, with less than 2\% relative WER degradation. Direct activity prediction increases these speedups to 79\% and 132\%, with relative WER degradations of 10\% and 21\%, respectively.

title: Which Archived Results Survive a Rule Change? A Case Study in Revalidating Decisions
summary: A research workflow can retain a correct numerical result after the evidence or approval that supported its use has expired. Common incremental build methods identify reusable computations, while deciding what remains usable also requires knowing which policy justified each approval. We examined a recorded parser migration across 312 paired research records, replayed both parsers with the same inputs, applied a calculation-file omission to the complete cohort, and evaluated current proof in a GNU Make comparison. Treating the prior projections as current would change at least one field in 11 of 312 records, and controlled cases show that even matching values can lack a current proof. The study separates numerical recovery from applicable approval and sets out the conditions under which a maintained dependency graph can preserve both.

title: Exact Online $Q_n$ Estimation: Exploiting Sliding-Window Rank Invariance
summary: The $Q_n$ scale estimator (Rousseeuw and Croux, 1993) combines a 50% finite-sample breakdown point with high Gaussian efficiency, but its computation requires selecting an order statistic among the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairwise distances. We study exact online $Q_n$ computation in a sliding window by exploiting temporal rank coherence between consecutive windows. Formalizing the multiset decomposition of surviving pairwise distances in terms of strict and weak rank counts, we derive a tie-exact dual-rank update that verifies whether the previous unscaled estimate remains valid in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ comparisons while maintaining the sorted window in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time. When the target rank shifts by $m$ positions, a localized row-heap procedure initialized via a monotonic two-pointer frontier scan extracts the new exact order statistic in $\mathcal{O}(n + m\log n)$ comparisons without materializing the difference matrix, complemented by a hybrid fallback that executes frontier-guided implicit matrix selection in $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ time for larger rank shifts. On deterministic multi-regime stress streams, our implementation matches the offline batch reference. In repeated same-platform benchmarks on a synthetic Gaussian stream, our implementation achieves median internal throughputs from 2,220,000 updates/s ($n=25$) and 1,140,000 updates/s ($n=51$) to 127,000 updates/s ($n=201$), outperforming both the exact FQN baseline ($2.5\times$ to $6.4\times$) and the approximate AFQN sketch ($1.3\times$ to $2.7\times$) across all tested window sizes.

title: Connectivity-Constrained Linear System Realization: Feasibility and Realizable Sets
summary: In this paper, we first study the problem of finding a state-space realization of a given transfer function that adheres to a given connectivity pattern (i.e., support). While variants of this problem have been studied in distributed and structured control, existing work typically focuses on connectivity patterns relating to some networked plant. In contrast, we are interested in arbitrary connectivity patterns, which are relevant to modeling problems in sensorimotor neuroscience. We show that this problem is equivalent to solving a system of multivariate polynomial equations, and can be solved exactly without relaxation or approximation. We then study the reverse problem: given a connectivity pattern, what transfer functions have a state-space realization that adheres to this pattern? In other words, what transfer functions can this pattern realize? A surprising finding is that any given pattern can realize nearly all transfer functions, or very few transfer functions. We provide rigorous results and algorithms for both problems, leveraging technical machinery from algebraic geometry. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated in examples at the end of the paper.

title: How developers split roles among them and a coding agent and what "collaboration" means
comment: 32 pages (plus 27 pages of appendices), 4 figures, 10 tables
summary:
Background: Coding agents such as Claude Code become more and more competent, so that their role in the development process can grow.
  Objective: How do developers characterize the role-split between them and their agent? How would they ideally want to collaborate with their agent?
  Methods: We perform a 3-step, mixed-methods study. We apply qualitative open coding to 2025 early adopters' blog articles; perform a quantitative survey of 2026 practitioners; develop and apply a method for coding-agent-supported open coding of survey freetext responses.
  Results: The 2025 practitioners have the agent work in supporting roles only. Accountability was firmly human. In 2026, both are fundamentally still true. Gradually, however, the role-split is now different, with much more agent involvement. The developers' notion of collaboration has three facets: Predominantly a separation into human-only, agent-only, and collaborative work steps, with defined conditions and goals. Second, accommodating personal preferences without engineering justification. Third, a holistic view of collaboration covering the entire development process.
  Conclusions: Defining one's role relative to the agent will need to be a recurring activity. The different views on collaboration are likely a source of friction and conflict for teams; future work should find out how to cope with that.

title: Estimating contextual networks via Fisher-scoring surrogate likelihood
summary: When networks are accompanied by vertex-level covariates, effectively integrating and aligning the information underlying both data sources becomes a natural yet critical task. Current spectral approaches, despite their popularity, may yield suboptimal results and necessitate the specification of additional tuning parameters that are contingent upon unobservable signal-to-noise ratios. We propose a tuning-free, likelihood-based learning framework for estimating latent positions in contextual generalized random dot product graphs in the presence of high-dimensional vertex covariates with a low-rank structure. Our method constructs a smooth surrogate likelihood and implements a Fisher-scoring algorithm to iteratively estimate latent positions without introducing additional tuning parameters that depend on the network sparsity. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the Fisher-scoring estimator. Application to real-world data further demonstrates the method's practical utility, offering a principled and scalable alternative to spectral approaches for analyzing contextual networks in high-dimensional settings.

title: $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Grid-Forming Control in DC Microgrids
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics
summary: The growing share of DC-based generation, storage and loads has increased interest in DC microgrids. As a result, DC-bus voltage regulation and stability have become active research topics, with considerable effort directed at improving the transient performance of conventional droop control. Although numerous variants of droop algorithms have been proposed, many rely on increasingly complex control structures with multiple tuning parameters and measurements, thereby increasing the commissioning burden. Moreover, stable interaction with the surrounding microgrid is not guaranteed by design. To address these issues, this paper develops a passivity-constrained $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ synthesis method for the DC-bus voltage controller. The proposed $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ controller emulates the desired grid-forming behavior of the converter by minimizing the $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ error norm between device-level performance indices and their desired values, while additionally enforcing passivity during the optimization. The novel $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ control scheme is benchmarked in the frequency domain against representative droop-based and virtual-DC-machine algorithms from the literature, while experiments on a four-converter DC microgrid corroborate the frequency-domain analysis and validate the practical applicability of the algorithm.

title: On the loss landscape of the linear neural network: beyond critical points
summary: While the critical points of the loss landscape in linear neural networks have been extensively studied since the seminal work of Baldi \& Hornik in the late 1980s, a description of this landscape at an intermediate or global scale is still lacking. Such a characterization is crucial, particularly as a substantial body of literature indicates that gradient descent circumvents critical points. The present article introduces an intermediate structure, termed the critical thalweg, which encompasses all critical points and exhibits key geometric properties. Beyond providing a geometric proof of Baldi \& Hornik's results using simpler assumptions than the existing literature, this framework offers a global view of the loss landscape that can be easily visualized in a two-dimensional plane. Empirical observations suggest that gradient descent is attracted toward the critical thalweg, along which the loss continues to decrease to its global minimum.

title: Estimating conditional means under missingness-not-at-random with incomplete auxiliary variables
summary:
Estimators assuming missingness at random (MAR) can fail under missingness not at random (MNAR). Introducing complete auxiliary variables sometimes restores MAR by breaking dependence between analysis variables and missingness. However, if the auxiliaries are themselves incomplete, MAR typically remains violated.
  We derive necessary and sufficient, weaker-than-MAR conditions under which the MAR functional $μ_{\rm MAR}$ for a conditional mean $E[Y \mid X]$ is correct. We also propose an alternative identifying functional for $E[Y \mid X]$, called $μ_{\rm MIA}$ for "Marginalization over Incomplete Auxiliaries", along with sufficient conditions for $μ_{\rm MIA}$ to be correct.
  For MNAR distributions in which all missingness patterns can occur and certain context-specific independences do not occur, there are two straightforward cases where $μ_{\rm MIA}$ is correct for a strict superset of the MNAR distributions for which $μ_{\rm MAR}$ is correct: (1) $X$ is complete and $Y$ is incomplete; or (2) all auxiliary variables are incomplete. In case (1), $μ_{\rm MAR}$ is always incorrect, barring knife-edge cases. Determining whether either case holds requires no knowledge of the MNAR mechanism.
  We propose estimators of $μ_{\rm MIA}$, including g-computation and doubly robust estimators. Our R package miapack implements a semiparametric iterated-conditional-expectations estimator. We illustrate with real data and present simulations comparing estimators of $μ_{\rm MIA}$ and $μ_{\rm MAR}$.

title: A High-Compression Transformer VAE for Efficient and Controllable 3D Medical Image Generation with Diffusion Transformers
summary: Many medical image processing tasks, such as completing missing regions or correcting acquisition artifacts, can be cast as volumetric generation conditioned on observations of the same patient. Diffusion Transformers offer scalable capacity and flexible conditioning for this setting, but they operate on a learned image representation that must preserve fine anatomical and pathological detail while keeping complete three-dimensional volumes tractable. We bring Transformer variational autoencoding and multimodal diffusion together to address this challenge. Trained on BrainTumor-256K, a 249M Transformer VAE encodes and decodes $256^3$ volumes 7.6x faster than a comparably sized CNN trained on the same collection. Their PSNR difference is near zero with training-sized crop inputs, but the Transformer leads by 0.749 dB with full-volume inputs and an unchanged scoring region. Increasing Transformer capacity to 499M improves PSNR across all four brain MRI evaluation sets while retaining 3.8x lower encoding-decoding latency than the CNN. Fast encoding also allows conditions to be constructed dynamically in image space during latent diffusion training. Within the compressed representation, a shared Diffusion Transformer integrates text and spatial references for volumetric synthesis, completion and restoration. The brain-trained autoencoder further transfers to non-brain MRI and CT without target-domain fine-tuning, extending its use beyond the anatomy and modality on which it was learned. The framework provides a reusable representation and conditioning interface for efficient, controllable medical image generation. Code is available at https://github.com/OncoMMAI/brainmri-vit-vae3d.

title: Cohomological $k$-Equivalence Does Not Capture Graph Isomorphism
comment: 21 pages. The ancillary files contain the code and the logs of the finite checks described in the appendix
summary:
Ó Conghaile introduced cohomological $k$-equivalence $\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k$, a refinement of equivalence in $k$-variable counting logic that is decidable in polynomial time for each fixed $k$: the local isomorphisms that survive must extend, in both directions, to compatible families of integer combinations of local isomorphisms. He asked whether, for every finite relational signature $σ$, some $k$ makes $\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k$ coincide with isomorphism of $σ$-structures (Question 14 of his MFCS 2022 paper). We show that the answer is negative already for graphs: for every $k\ge 1$ there are finite simple graphs $A_k\not\cong B_k$ with $A_k\equiv^{\mathbb{Z}}_k B_k$.
  Every isomorphism of the pair would induce a permutation $g$ of a common index set $D$. One part of the graphs, over $\mathbb{F}_3$, admits exactly the even permutations, because $g$ acts by its sign on a nonzero class in the cokernel of the unsigned boundary map on subsets of $D$. A second part, over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and built on the Johnson graph $J(|D|,2)$, admits exactly the odd permutations. No set of at most $k$ vertices detects the parity: every local isomorphism of a common family is realised, with the same images, by permutations of both parities.
  We complement the main result with three observations. For the pair built from an index set of size $n$, the least width at which cohomological equivalence distinguishes the two graphs is $\log_4 n+O(1)$; so within this construction the doubly exponential size is unavoidable. The pairs are nevertheless distinguished in polynomial time by an explicit invariant that combines the class of the part over $\mathbb{F}_3$ with the parity of the part over $\mathbb{F}_2$. Finally, cohomological $2$-equivalence already distinguishes the coloured graphs with which Berkholz and Grohe show that no level of the Diophantine relaxation decides isomorphism.

title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm
summary: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.

title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Power Systems. Code: https://github.com/MFHChehade/loop-opf
summary: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

title: One Behavior, Out of Order: Deterministic Execution and Parallel Simulation of ROS 2 Applications
summary: System-level simulation is widely used to validate robotic applications before hardware deployment. However, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), a popular middleware for such applications, uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, which can make application behavior depend on scheduling and the platform. The behavior can then vary across runs and machines even with the same inputs. This nondeterminism makes faults hard to reproduce and tests unreliable. In this paper, we first give ROS 2 applications a lightweight coordination scheme in which every component, including event-driven ones, reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants. By decoupling computation and communication, the scheme makes an application deterministic, that is, it always has one behavior for given inputs. Tests are thus repeatable, but for large applications they still take a long time. To speed up these tests, we then present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm. From the predefined read and write instants, it knows before the run which activations of components depend on which. It starts each activation as soon as those it depends on have finished. Finally, we implement the algorithm in a simulator that runs existing ROS 2 applications without any change to them or to ROS 2. We evaluate the simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs. On the industrial use cases, it is up to 2.6 times faster than synchronous parallel simulation and needs an order of magnitude less memory for messages than asynchronous parallel simulation.

title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
comment: 20 pages (13 pages main text and a 7-page supplement), 8 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation
summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

title: On Pareto-Optimal Estimation-Information Limits-Achieving Distributions for Integrated Sensing and Communications
summary: ISAC systems enable simultaneous data transmission and environmental sensing using a common waveform. Characterizing their fundamental estimation-information performance limits is of core interest in information theory. In this paper, the achievable data rate for communications and the Miller-Chang-type CRB on sensing distortion are adopted as ISAC performance metrics, both of which are functionals of the ISAC waveform distribution. Our aim is to characterize the optimal input distributions across the entire CRB-rate Pareto boundary, corresponding to different sensing-communication tradeoff preferences. Three types of power constraint on input waveform are considered, namely, i) general power (GP), ii) maximum amplitude (MA), and iii) constant modulus (CM) constraints. Under these constraints, Pareto-optimal input distributions are shown to exhibit a common structural property: the directional component is uniformly distributed over the complex unit sphere; the power distribution is discrete (excluding the communication-optimal point under GP, where it follows a Gamma distribution induced by Gaussian inputs). We further investigate and characterize their Pareto-optimal sensing-communication preference dependent support structures. Finally, numerical algorithms are developed under GP and MA to trace their Pareto boundaries and determine corresponding optimal power distributions based on their respective support characteristics. From both analytical and numerical results, we conclude sensing prefers deterministic power while communication benefits from a richer distribution of power levels, thereby revealing the sensing-communication waveform uncertainty tradeoff in the fundamental power domain.

title: Puzzles, People, and Publications: Measuring Shared Significance in Crosswords from 1942 to 2024
summary: Crossword puzzles are cultural objects that encode shared significance. We use interpretable, large-scale computational methods to analyze how crossword constructors, editors, and publications have adopted and adapted language to convey significance. Focusing on approximately 2.4 million crossword clue/answer pairs published in The New York Times between 1942 and 2024, we find shifting significance and differing editorial practices to be quantitatively measurable. By computationally measuring shared significance over time in crossword puzzle production, we are able to better understand cultural changes in the United States through the 20th and early 21st centuries.

title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
summary: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.

title: Mode Recommendation and Dynamic Routing Guidance for Improved Trip Quality in Mixed Traffic Networks
summary: Urban mixed traffic networks provide diverse mobility options, yet conventional routing guidance with fixed travel modes leaves the benefits of coordinating travel modes and route planning largely unexploited. This paper proposes an integrated mode recommendation and dynamic routing guidance framework for urban mixed traffic networks comprising private vehicles, autonomous vehicles, and buses. We formulate a dynamic trip index (DTX) that incorporates mode-specific travel time, monetary cost, and convenience, enabling consistent evaluation of trip quality across travel modes. Using this measure, we develop a mode recommendation method that selects feasible autonomous vehicle or bus services based on predicted DTX for travelers without private vehicles, while preserving service capacity for travelers with known demand. We integrate this method with dynamic routing guidance for private and autonomous vehicles to improve the average trip quality of all travelers. Simulation studies involving $1{,}500$ travelers on a real-world road network in Shanghai, China, show that the proposed framework increases the mean realized DTX by $13.01\%$ compared with dynamic routing guidance alone and by $19.68\%$ compared with fixed travel modes with preplanned routes, highlighting the value of mode flexibility in improving trip quality beyond route adaptation.

title: A posteriori estimates for inverse evolutionary problems
summary: The paper is focused on a posteriori error analysis of evolutionary problems, which are ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard. They may have no solutions and respective approximations may be highly unstable. For these problems, the a posteriori error estimation concept applicable to well-posed problems is not valid and requires a significant reformulation. A posteriori estimates of the functional type provide the basis for addressing this issue. They generate computable quantities that estimate the distance between a function (approximate solution to the inverse problem) and exact solution of a "close" well-posed initial boundary value problem associated with the same differential equation. The solution of this close problem exactly satisfies one part of the imposed conditions and the others are satisfied approximately with the accuracy $\eps$. This idea is elaborated for several evolutionary problems generated by the reaction-convection-diffusion equation: backward parabolic problem, problem with non-local time conditions, Cauchy parabolic problem, and parameter(s) identification problem. The estimates derived not only control the accuracy of approximate solutions, but also suggest a unified approach to calculating them numerically.

title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data
summary: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on Pólya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

title: Particle picking with an earth mover's seminorm
summary: Particle picking is a key step in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy. It is a challenging task where tomographic projections of proteins and other macromolecules are identified in extremely noisy images. In this work, we introduce a particle picker based on a seminorm defined in terms of a fast wavelet approximation to the earth mover's distance. Our picker is template-free, self-supervised and does not require any prior knowledge of the molecules of interest other than their approximate size. We test it on three public datasets and show that it achieves state-of-the-art reconstructions.

title: Model the Annotation, Not the Noise: Semantic Annotation-Channel Prompt Learning against Noisy Labels
summary: Parameter-efficient prompt learning has become a cornerstone for adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs), yet it remains highly vulnerable to label noise in few-shot Web and retrieval scenarios. Existing noise robust methods typically rely on hard sample selection or deterministic label correction, which discard valuable semantic ambiguity and overlook how observed annotations are actually generated. To bridge this gap, we reformulate noisy prompt learning through the perspective of data generation, proposing SACP, a Semantic-aware Annotation Channel-based Prompt learning framework. Instead of suppressing noise heuristically, SACP decouples latent clean-label prediction from instance-dependent annotation generation. By integrating frozen VLM semantic priors with lightweight visual residuals, SACP constructs a structured annotation channel optimized via generalized expectation-maximization with soft posteriors. Furthermore, a posterior-aware memory is introduced to preserve label uncertainty during test-time inference. Extensive experiments across different synthetic benchmarks and the real-world noisy Food101N dataset demonstrate that SACP achieves state-of-the-art performance against its counterparts in different label noise patterns, especially under severe asymmetric noise.

title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator
summary: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

title: FM4SAR-Bench 1.0: Towards A Fair Benchmark for Evaluating Foundation Models for SAR Image Interpretation
summary: Foundation models have advanced SAR image interpretation but created a heterogeneous, fragmented model ecosystem. Existing models differ substantially in their input, training data, objectives, architectures, and release policy, yet the field lacks a unified taxonomy and comparative framework. Current evaluations rely primarily on task-specific benchmarks, which are ill-suited to fair comparison among models with fundamentally different input-output formats and task paradigms, and often overlook data transparency, reproducibility, interpretability, and deployment readiness. Limited SAR data accessibility also means high reported performance does not guarantee access to training data, code, or weights, limiting reproduction, benchmarking, and deployment. To address these issues, we propose a systematic taxonomy and hierarchical evaluation framework for SAR-related foundation models: five rating levels, six dimensions, and fine-grained criteria, with separate protocols for VFMs and VLMs. Beyond overall ratings, it yields interpretable multidimensional capability profiles and supports user-defined weighting, so rankings follow user priorities. Utilizing a fixed auxiliary multimodal large language model in combination with human review, we conduct a systematic meta-analysis and multidimensional assessment of 76 VFMs and 40 VLMs. In terms of SAR benchmark task performance under our framework, SAR-native VLMs do not significantly outperform remote sensing VLMs pretrained on mixed multimodal corpora in which SAR is one of several modalities. This lack of clear advantage is largely due to data availability: large-scale, high-quality, public annotated SAR data remain scarce, restricting both model and training-data scale for SAR-native models. The framework provides a structured basis for requirement-aware model selection and remains extensible as new models emerge.

title: Latent Space Planning with Sequential Monte Carlo
summary: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.

title: Beware of complexity bias: A hindrance to conceptual model generalization and interpretability
summary: In the field of rainfall-runoff modeling, lumped conceptual models have been shown to be powerful representations of catchment filtering functions. They demonstrate fairly strong predictive performance in gauged catchments and have the ability to learn important intermediate latent variables and flow paths which increases their value as interpretable models. During calibration, these conceptual models may fit streamflow just as well as deep learning models, however, their performance often sharply degrades after deployment, suggesting the presence of overfitting. We hypothesize that complexity (or flexibility) bias is one of the causes of such overfitting. Complexity bias can appear within conceptual models when the number of effective degrees of freedom is parameter or flow path dependent. Using a popular conceptual model and a series of synthetic datasets, we illustrate the presence of complexity bias and demonstrate its impact on model interpretability/parameter inference. Then, using real rainfall-runoff data from CAMELS-US, we investigate if overfitting can be reduced by adding regularization terms that prevent complexity bias from forming. Our results suggest that conceptual and hybrid modeling can be further improved if hydrologists become aware of this pervasive bias.

title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Companion dataset included as ancillary files
summary: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.

title: Federated KPI Aggregation with Local Privacy Constraints and Coordinated OLAP Roll-Ups
comment: Presented at 2026 13th International Conference on Soft Computing & Machine Intelligence (ISCMI 2026), November 2026. Accepted for publication in the conference proceedings. Official publication forthcoming
summary: Cross-organizational KPI analysis can require aggregated results from independently administered data warehouses without centralizing detailed records. To limit disclosure from small local groups, a site can require a minimum number of contributing records before releasing a KPI value for a group. If each site applies this rule independently, different local contributions may be suppressed and the combined KPI can become incomplete. This paper investigates whether OLAP granularity can be coordinated before local query results are released so that all sites satisfy their local minimum-cohort rules and contribute at the same analytical level. The proposed method selects the least-generalized common roll-up accepted by every site. Site agents coordinate current capabilities and approved local execution across independently administered sites, with privacy checks and aggregate computation remaining deterministic local functions. In a four-site prototype, coordinated roll-up retained all contributions and reproduced the corresponding centralized result, compared with 78.3% retained under independent suppression. A capability-change experiment showed fewer candidate checks and replies and no unsupported requests when current site-agent state was used. The results demonstrate the feasibility of federated KPI aggregation under local privacy constraints through coordinated granularity selection and agent-based coordination.

title: graphMTP: An R Shiny Interface for Graphical Multiple Testing and Interim Monitoring
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Related conference version: https://zenodo.org/records/23272972
summary: Graphical multiple testing procedures provide a framework for controlling the family-wise error rate across endpoints, treatment comparisons, and patient populations in confirmatory clinical trials. Interim monitoring requires analysts to track changing local significance levels together with hypothesis-specific testing schedules. We present graphMTP, an R application built with shiny, for constructing hypothesis graphs, specifying per-hypothesis group-sequential plans, and inspecting alpha recycling. The application uses TrialSimulator for graph updates, gsDesign for spending profiles, and rpact for boundary calculations. It records the local levels, boundaries, and decisions used for each submitted test and exports designs and histories as JSON files. Worked examples cover fixed-design reallocation, fixed-sequence gatekeeping, delayed activation, and retesting a previously monitored recipient of alpha. Replication code checks graph updates, normal crossing probabilities, and saved-session replay. Sequential tests use a prespecified information schedule and reconstruct the complete local boundary family at the current allocation, including after recycling. Historical event records retain the boundaries actually used. An installable package and standalone sources accompany the article.

title: Hybrid-Field Interference Suppression for Low-Complexity Uplink Channel Estimation
summary: Uplink channel estimation can be severely degraded by hybrid-field interference, where strong near-field intra-site interference is coupled with far-field inter-site interference. Although a joint near-/far-field dictionary can capture this interference structure, it requires dense angle--distance matching that may incur high complexity and performance degradation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a hybrid-field interference suppression framework for uplink channel estimation. First, we formulate a hybrid-field interference model and analyze its sparse reconstruction. Then, to avoid exhaustive near-field dictionary matching, we propose a low-complexity interference-parameter estimation method based on the angle--domain diffusion pattern of the dominant interference. Using the estimated parameters, the proposed parametric interference-nulling orthogonal matching pursuit (PIN-OMP) algorithm suppresses the dominant interference components and reconstructs the desired uplink channel from the interference-suppressed observation. Furthermore, a physical critical-distance bound is derived to characterize the feasible distance-inversion region, and a conditional hybrid Cram'er--Rao bound (HCRB) is established to quantify the desired channel reconstruction limit under a reconstructed interference basis. Finally, numerical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

title: Parasite Features: Causal Abstraction Through Spurious Pathways
summary: Causal Abstraction defines a notion of \emph{equivalence} between a neural network and an algorithm, thus serving as a powerful framework for mechanistic interpretability. In this paper, however, we show the existence of a class of \emph{spurious features} which straightforwardly pass such equivalence tests. Suppose there are two directions in a model's representation space where: (i) one discriminates the input based on some feature, and (ii) the other steers the model towards a certain output. Interpretability methods based on Causal Abstraction (e.g., Distributed Alignment Search) can \emph{spuriously} simulate these directions' combined behavior by leveraging pathways passing through them, giving the impression that the model implements this feature. In such cases, we say the method discovered a \defn{parasite feature}. Experimentally, we show that Distributed Alignment Search finds parasite features using linear alignment maps in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. Our paper highlights an important consideration for Causal Abstraction and contributes to the ongoing debate about best practices for mechanistic interpretability.

title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
summary: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.

title: Dem2TA: Beyond Pixels, Towards Perception
summary: Task-oriented image signal processors (ISPs) adapt RAW-to-RGB processing for downstream perception. However, explicit demosaicing is often simplified, kept fixed, or optimized primarily for reconstruction quality, leaving this stage insufficiently integrated into task adaptation. We propose \textbf{Dem2TA}, a framework that incorporates fidelity-supervised demosaicing into the adaptation of the perception pipeline. Starting from a pretrained demosaicing model, we jointly adapt the reconstruction frontend and downstream network using reconstruction and task supervision, together with complementary semantic and task representation alignment. We then freeze the adapted frontend and jointly optimize a lightweight local ISP with the downstream model to refine task-specific rendering without changing the reconstructed linear RGB. Experiments on synthetic RAW detection and box-prompted segmentation demonstrate the effectiveness of representation-guided joint adaptation and subsequent local rendering. Evaluation on a manually verified real-capture dataset further supports transfer beyond synthetic inputs. Compared with TA-ISP on the same adapted foundation, Dem2TA improves detection AP by 0.46 points and segmentation IoU by 1.06 points on synthetic COCO RAW, and segmentation IoU by 0.63 points on real captures.

title: Forehead ROI Localization under Real-World Imaging Degradations via Cross-View Pseudo-Labeling
comment: 9 pages, submitted and accepted to the 2027 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW)
summary: Forehead region-of-interest (ROI) localization is important for forehead-creases biometrics, particularly when the lower face is occluded. However, localization remains challenging under varying image quality, pose, and illumination. We propose Confidence and Consistency Guided Pseudo-Labeling (CCGP), which adapts Grounding DINO using unlabeled facial images filtered by detection confidence and geometric consistency between original and horizontally flipped views, without modifying the detector architecture or loss. We evaluate CCGP on five external datasets and 350 images spanning seven imaging conditions. CCGP achieves the highest mean intersection over union (mIoU) on four of five external datasets, improving from 0.415 to 0.580 on RMFRD compared with supervised Grounding DINO. On the quality-stratified subset, the largest gains occur under blur (0.487 to 0.719) and low contrast (0.615 to 0.710). CCGP also outperforms conventional self-training on RMFRD (0.580 versus 0.551 mIoU). Despite a slight in-domain performance gap (0.861 vs. 0.866 mIoU) and challenges with off-angle poses, CCGP improves cross-dataset localization under challenging imaging conditions.

title: Smoothed Conformal Testing with Small Calibration Sets
summary: A small calibration sample restricts split conformal $p$-values to a coarse rank grid. Randomization removes this discretization, but its effect depends on both the smoothing interval and the allocation of auxiliary random variables. Independent tie-block randomization is exactly valid under null exchangeability. When calibration and null scores are jointly exchangeable conditional on the alternative scores, we prove positive regression dependence and hence Benjamini--Hochberg false discovery rate control, including for atomic score distributions. Smoothing over calibration-dependent rank cells agrees with tie-block randomization when calibration scores are distinct and no test score ties a calibration score, but can fail marginal validity with atoms. Assigning sorted random draws according to score order can invalidate even a single null $p$-value. An exact two-test example violates the usual $π_0α$ bound, and simulations with continuous scores exhibit false discovery rates above the nominal level $α$. Finally, conditional moment identities and normal-model illustrations show that removing the rank grid does not remove calibration uncertainty. Randomization can produce additional discoveries, including when ordinary conformal testing cannot reject at all, but it does not generally substitute for a larger calibration sample.

title: ECG-LabWAS: A Laboratory-Wide Association Study Using a Fine-Tuned Single-Lead Electrocardiogram Foundation Model
summary: Laboratory testing guides clinical diagnosis but requires blood sampling and processing. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is fast and noninvasive and may carry information about laboratory abnormalities, yet most AI-ECG models target one test at a time using 12-lead recordings. We conducted an exploratory ECG laboratory-wide association study (ECG-LabWAS), fine-tuning an ECG foundation model pretrained on 10.8 million ECGs to screen 50 laboratory tests from single-lead waveforms alone. The model was developed in an emergency-department cohort (MC-MED; 31,826 patients) and applied unchanged to an independent hospital cohort (MIMIC-IV; 115,921 patients). Of 89 abnormality directions (low or high values of each test), 33 met the same screening criteria in both cohorts. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve in the two cohorts were 0.841 and 0.838 for elevated NT-proBNP, 0.769 and 0.740 for elevated cardiac troponin, 0.755 and 0.731 for elevated creatinine, and 0.713 and 0.710 for low potassium. Discrimination changed little when the ECG--laboratory matching window was widened from $\pm$1 to $\pm$24 hours. Model predictions reproduced the co-occurrence of observed abnormalities but were about twice as tightly coupled, largely along one shared component consistent with overall illness severity; low potassium, elevated NT-proBNP and troponin, and markers of renal function retained discrimination beyond that of correlated tests. In exploratory analyses, ECG-assisted versions of the modified Glasgow Prognostic Score and the systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria were associated with in-hospital and one-year mortality. These results identify which laboratory abnormalities warrant analyte-specific study with single-lead ECG.

title: SCATR-ITS: a scalable transformer for large-area individual tree segmentation from LiDAR point clouds
summary: Individual tree segmentation (ITS) from LiDAR point clouds is one of the most widely studied segmentation tasks in forestry. Although deep learning methods define the state of the art on the majority of ITS benchmarks, their high computational complexity and long runtime currently prevent their adoption in large-scale operational workflows. In this work, we present SCATR-ITS, a scalable transformer model specifically designed for efficient ITS over large geographical areas. Based on the ForestFormer3D framework, SCATR-ITS transitions to superpoint-level processing to accelerate inference, with the superpoints constructed from learned embeddings. The architecture incorporates size-aware superpoint-level postprocessing, a dynamic query count module to handle high variation in forest structure, and a maximal input stride designed to minimize prediction redundancy. SCATR-ITS achieves accuracy on par with the state of the art on the FGI-EMIT and FOR-InstanceV2 datasets with an up to 8.5$\times$ higher inference speed. In addition, SCATR-ITS has a significantly lower GPU VRAM footprint during both training and inference, and exhibits excellent zero-shot generalization across multiple datasets. To demonstrate large-area ITS capabilities, SCATR-ITS is applied to a 142 km$^2$ region of Finnish national laser scanning data where it achieves an average throughput of 13.8 min/km$^2$, $\sim$18.6$\times$ faster than ForestFormer3D and approaching the speed of the unsupervised watershed algorithm, which it vastly outperforms in accuracy and segment quality. Overall, SCATR-ITS delivers state-of-the-art accuracy at speeds where operational-scale adoption becomes viable, paving the way toward countrywide deployment. The source code for SCATR-ITS and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/ruoppa/scatr_its.

title: Adaptive Redescending Regression with $q$-Polynomial Losses
summary: We introduce a family of smooth $q$-polynomial losses for robust joint regression--scale estimation. The family contains the Cauchy loss at $q=1$ and converges pointwise to the squared loss as $q$ increases. For every finite $q$, its regression score is bounded and redescending, while its scale score is bounded and permits explicit analysis of scale existence. We formulate simultaneous estimation through a surrogate likelihood with a common scale calibration $κ=1/2$ and select $q$ by maximizing the normalized surrogate likelihood over a finite candidate set. We investigate existence, large-sample behaviour, and the robustness implications of the loss family and discuss how optional modification of the scale score, for example by taking $κ=q/2$, can increase the threshold against scale explosion. This breakdown-oriented adjustment is distinct from the baseline estimator and requires its own joint breakdown analysis. An MM-type algorithm provides a practical implementation. Numerical investigations assess the resulting robustness--efficiency trade-off under different tail regimes.

title: Strong Functional Observability and Strong Functional Detectability: Applications to Functional Observer Design for Systems with Unknown Inputs
summary: This paper investigates strong functional observability, strong functional detectability, and strong$^*$ functional detectability for continuous-time linear systems with unknown inputs in both the state and measurement equations. Extending Kratz's finite algebraic approach \cite{26}, zero-output trajectories are characterized through the projected kernel of a finite matrix, without differentiating the unknown inputs. This characterization yields a necessary and sufficient rank condition for strong functional observability. For strong functional detectability, a frequency-dependent rank criterion involving only the original system matrices is derived, along with an equivalent finite test based on reduced zero-output dynamics. Strong$^*$ functional detectability is then characterized by an additional algebraic rank condition, and its relationship with the existence of stable functional observers is examined. A constructive observer design procedure based on constrained Sylvester equations is also developed. Particular cases and a numerical process example illustrate the theoretical results.

title: Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary material (Sections S-I through S-X)
summary: Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erdős-Rényi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.

title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach
summary: Firms routinely conduct randomized experiments, creating archives that could improve treatment-effect estimation in new experiments. However, past experiments evaluate related but different interventions, so their estimates may be biased for the current target. We study when and how borrowing from multiple auxiliary experiments can reduce the mean squared error (MSE) of a single treatment-effect estimate. In the oracle case, when biases and variances are known, borrowing from even one biased experiment strictly reduces MSE. In practice, we propose three shrinkage estimators and characterize their asymptotic MSE as the number of auxiliary experiments grows. Our analysis shows that average auxiliary bias and cross-study bias dispersion affect the relative performance of these estimators. As expected, smaller average bias magnitude generally improves performance. Surprisingly, bias dispersion can both benefit and harm our first estimator, the general plug-in estimator. On one hand, a more dispersed bias allows flexibility in cancelling the bias. On the other hand, the bias cancellation is imperfect as we only have an estimate of the bias, leading to overfitting. Motivated by this tradeoff, we propose a pooled plug-in estimator that restricts study-specific reweighting to limit this overfitting. However, both plug-in estimators can perform poorly when average bias is large. To address this, we develop a fixed-weight estimator with a hypothesis-testing gate that borrows only when the aggregate auxiliary mean is not significantly different from the target mean. Simulations illustrate the relative strengths of these estimators across bias environments and the relevance of the limiting analysis for finite collections of experiments. We also provide managerial guidance on which shrinkage estimator to use based on average bias and bias dispersion.

title: PepDeTech: Anonymous Occupancy Monitoring on a Battery-Powered 2.3k-Zone dToF LiDAR Node with On-Chip Processing and Bluetooth LE Reporting
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: As populations grow, society is increasingly required to shift towards systems of shared resources, which allow space, energy and time to be optimised. Facilitating this transition depends on data: how many people are present, when and where. From such information, schedules can be organised more efficiently and resources allocated where they matter.
