We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.

title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code, dataset, and benchmark leaderboard available at https://egosurghands.github.io
summary: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io

title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/gezhixuan/opsis
summary: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. On 189 breast report questions, frontier models that read a written description of the slide or look at a thumbnail and tiles of it answer at 0.50 to 0.66, below the majority class at 0.67. A description is written before the question is known, and a look covers a handful of tiles. We present Opsis, which lets the model ask instead: a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder. A slide is encoded once, a question names an operator, arguments and candidates given at runtime, and the answer is a probability over the candidates. We build it as a 10 M parameter decoder on frozen Virchow2 tokens (Opsis-S) and inside Qwen3-VL-8B (Opsis-V). Asking Opsis-S, four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79, and on 3,797 pan cancer questions asking is 8.6 points above reading. On 995 composite questions that Opsis-S was never trained on, a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, against 0.69 when it looks at the slide and 0.78 for ABMIL trained on each composite. On a pan cancer question set over 10,712 TCGA slides, one Opsis-S decoder matches linear probes trained per question on TITAN and PRISM2 embeddings (average accuracy 0.69 against 0.70 and 0.68). Opsis-S also separates CAMELYON16 metastases without training on that cohort (AUROC 0.86) and localises necrosis from report labels alone (tile AUROC 0.93).

title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
summary:
Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference.
  We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference.
  In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.

title: Omo: Giving Continuing AI-Agent Work a Place to Return To
summary: AI coding agents now keep working while the people who started them are away. Coming back is the hard part: a session list tells you which agent is where, but not what it was asked to do, what it changed, or what to tell it next. We present Omo, which gives each piece of continuing agent work a persistent place to return to. We built the idea twice. Omo Space is an open-source Minecraft mod in which rooms and screens that people build are live terminals on their own machine. Omo Theia brings the same rooms and desks into a customizable IDE, one step away from the editor and the Git patch. Both keep agent sessions running on the host after the view is closed. We describe the two systems, four lessons from building them, and a study designed to test whether returning to a place helps people pick up agent work correctly.

title: Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure
summary: The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.

title: RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities through Agent Harness Evolution
summary: We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registration: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23608308. Results dataset: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24238904
summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

title: Federated and Balanced $k$-means: Communication Efficiency, Privacy, and Heterogeneity
summary: Collaborating on data across organizations in healthcare and finance demands methods that preserve privacy while enabling effective analysis. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates clustering across data where different parties hold different features of the same entities without sharing raw data. However, existing VFL clustering methods suffer from two key limitations: vulnerability to information leakage and the creation of imbalanced clusters. To address these limitations, we propose Fabric, a balanced and privacy-preserving federated $k$-means algorithm. Our method decomposes the balanced clustering problem into independent subproblems for each client, using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to efficiently handle the balance constraints. Under the semi-honest model, Fabric provides provable privacy guarantees by injecting calibrated noise into local objective evaluations. Extensive evaluations on ten real-world datasets show that Fabric achieves a superior utility-privacy trade-off compared with state-of-the-art methods and converges faster. Specifically, Fabric reduces SSE by 29.1\% on average and improves balance performance by 1.41$\times$, while being 26$\times$ faster on average.

title: A Footprint-Sensitive Cross-GPU Timing Channel Through the Shared Host Memory Subsystem
summary: Assigning tenants to separate GPUs does not isolate their host memory traffic. We identify an unprivileged timing channel between GPUs without NVLink: a co-tenant can detect contention by timing reads to its own pinned host buffer, without accessing victim data or using hardware performance counters. The signal tracks the number of distinct host pages the victim touches rather than its throughput. We demonstrate covert communication at 20 bit/s with near-zero error, LLM output-length inference at a held-out Spearman correlation of 0.99 across five models on three platforms, and refusal inference at balanced accuracy up to 0.955. The attacks cross process, container, and Unix-user boundaries and reproduce across two GPU generations and two serving runtimes. Bursty transfers in the tested vLLM+LMCache stack remain below the leakage floor, limiting the demonstrated attacks to sustained device-to-host traffic. IOMMU-disabled and cross-NUMA controls attribute the channel to page-walk contention at the shared host memory controller. This finding motivates two defenses, controller-aware placement and footprint flattening, both of which reduce inference to chance in our experiments. Accelerator isolation alone does not isolate the host infrastructure that tenants share.

title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
summary: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.

title: Highly Efficient Vertical Federated Clustering with Triangle-Inequality-based Pruning
summary: In many real-world scenarios, multiple parties hold complementary feature subsets for the same samples but cannot share raw data. This makes efficient clustering over distributed feature subsets an important and challenging problem. While vertical federated learning (VFL) enables such collaboration, existing VFL clustering methods often require many communication rounds or substantial local computation. To address these limitations, we first propose TriCD, an exact pruning method for CDKM that preserves the same cluster assignments under the same initialization. TriCD constructs triangle-inequality bounds on demand to skip redundant objective evaluations with negligible extra space. Building upon this, we propose FedTriCD, an efficient federated clustering algorithm. By decomposing the global objective into client-local subproblems, FedTriCD enables pruning-based local optimization using only local data. FedTriCD further reduces communication by allowing multiple local updates between server synchronizations. A proximal regularization term is introduced to control the drift caused by infrequent communication. Our theoretical analysis establishes the exactness and finite convergence of TriCD and provides a bounded-error server-side update guarantee for FedTriCD. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate the efficiency and clustering quality of the proposed methods. TriCD achieves up to a 50.07$\times$ speedup over \Lloyd's algorithm. Moreover, FedTriCD achieves competitive clustering quality while requiring fewer local evaluations and fewer communication rounds than state-of-the-art federated clustering methods.

title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.

title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
summary: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.

title: Drive Failure and Lifetime Simulation in the Backblaze Drive Statistics Corpus, 2013-2026
comment: 174 pages. Sustainable Systems Laboratory Technical Report SSL-TR-2026-001, Preprint v0.1
summary:
Storage simulators estimate data-loss risk from assumptions about drive lifetimes and dependence between failures. We test these assumptions against Backblaze's daily records from April 2013 to June 2026: 504,624 data drives with usable power-on ages, 99 drive models, 2.0 million drive-years and 31,881 recorded failures, including removals of drives judged likely to fail. We test failure-count forecasts over nine successive years and forecast the drives already in service at each prediction date.
  Accounting for drive-model differences and attributes improves the score assigned to observed failure counts about 4.3 times as much as replacing a single Weibull with two competing Weibulls under the same drive-model treatment. Fleet failure risk falls early and rises at older ages, but the fixed bathtub benchmark predicts 2.4 times the observed failures. Across 169 well-observed drive-model years selected using earlier records, 95% prediction intervals cover 44% of observed counts without annual variation and 92% with fleet-wide changes and shared good or bad years for each drive model.
  For drives already in service, a SMART warning raises one-year failure-risk ranking AUC from 0.64 to 0.73. Boosted trees using monthly SMART records give the best individual probability forecasts, yet predict 19% too many failures at one year and 22% too many at 90 days. Long-term survival depends on how aging is separated from calendar time: fitted fifteen-year survival probabilities differ by up to 18 percentage points, and assumptions about future calendar trends by up to 27 points. We provide samplers for storage simulations that represent drive-model differences, shared risks, and changes in drive condition.

title: Degree-stratified randomized projection for spectral clustering
summary: Many real-world networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions, in which a few high-degree nodes coexist with many low-degree nodes. Randomized range finders reduce the cost of computing the eigenspace used in spectral clustering, but their random test matrices are constructed independently of the node degrees. We propose degree-stratified randomized projection (DS-RP), which partitions the nodes into dyadic degree strata, distributes a fixed sketch dimension across the strata, and draws an independent local sketch for each stratum. We bound the angle between the sampled range and the target eigenspace and show that the gain comes from the allocation of the sketch dimension rather than from the stratification itself. The bound improves when more sketch dimensions are assigned to the strata on which the target eigenspace is concentrated. For the degree-corrected stochastic block model, we prove that the leverage scores of this eigenspace are proportional to the node degrees, so that the allocation can be determined from the degrees alone. A Rayleigh--Ritz bound that requires no smallness assumption carries the estimate over to the computed spectral embedding. Numerical experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world networks show that DS-RP improves the clustering accuracy of standard Gaussian and CountSketch projections at the same sketch dimension and essentially the same computational cost.

title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models
summary: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.

title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.

title: OpenRing: Deadlock-Free Execution of Any Planner on AGV Floors with One-Way Lanes
summary: Lifelong multi-agent path finding replans routes for automated guided vehicles, but deviations can invalidate a plan. With one-way lanes, a late vehicle or lost planner can close a ring of full segments. We separate how fast the floor runs from whether it keeps running. In OpenRing a planner proposes routes and an order, a local guard commits only moves and route changes that cannot close such a ring, and the order binds for a bounded time. Despite arbitrary proposals or planner loss, no ring closes. With two-place segments, traffic can continue under disturbances; progress is guaranteed once they end, and all vehicles exit if entries also stop. Among rules that reroute only on a proposal, every guard veto is necessary, and a clean plan keeps its crossing orders. The guarantee has a price: no rule that never stores a vehicle in a crossing under arbitrary stops carries more than $B/T_s$ per segment of $B$ places and traversal time $T_s$. With binding orders, three planners deadlock in 80 of 126 runs across eight floors. Inside OpenRing, none of the 126 runs deadlocks. OpenRing's closed-loop throughput rivals or exceeds the best baseline's. Physics simulations show no deadlocks or overlaps.

title: Analyzing Multi-Layer Visual Representations of Large Vision-Language Models for Anomaly Detection
summary: In this paper, we analyze multi-layer visual representations in large vision-language models (LVLMs) and examine the effectiveness of layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion for anomaly detection. Representative LVLMs connect visual encoder features to a language model through a projector. In this design, deep visual encoder features carry high-level semantics and alignment with text representations, whereas shallow and intermediate layers retain information relevant to vision-centric tasks, such as local appearance and fine-grained shape. It is therefore important to choose layer representations and fusion methods according to the nature of the downstream task. Focusing on anomaly detection, we compare layer-wise features and multi-layer fusion across multiple supervision levels and a variety of classifiers, and examine from several perspectives how multi-layer visual representations affect downstream performance. By analyzing the resulting performance differences, we further discuss the contribution of each layer representation to anomaly detection and provide empirical insights into representation selection for vision-centric tasks.

title: Opto-Electronic Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Based on MZI for Robotic Manipulator Control
summary: Precise motion control for autonomous robots is a core technical enabler for the large-scale deployment of embodied intelligence. In particular, basic manipulation tasks, such as point-to-point reaching and target grasping with robotic manipulators, impose stringent requirements on control accuracy, real-time response, and energy efficiency for edge deployment. As a prevailing end-to-end control paradigm, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous learning and generalization for decision-making in continuous action spaces. Nevertheless, constrained by electronic computing architectures, it generally suffers from substantial computing overhead, high inference latency and limited energy efficiency, making low-power edge deployment challenging. Optical computing, benefiting from its high-speed parallelism, offers a promising route to break energy-efficiency bottlenecks; however, research on the integration of optical computing and RL remains at an early stage. In this work, we propose a Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI)-based opto-electronic hybrid RL architecture. We adopted two algorithm structures: Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with Hindsight Experience Replay (DDPG-HER) and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with HER (TD3-HER). We implemented the key layer linear computation of the spiking neural network (SNN) Actor on an optical MZI chip for the reaching task of a Franka Emika Panda robotic manipulator. The architecture is evaluated in the PyBullet simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves an energy efficiency of 1.39 TOPS/W and an inference latency of 120ps while maintaining control accuracy, which provide a feasible pathway toward energy-efficient and precise control for robots.

title: Spatiotemporal Landslide Runout Reconstruction from Sparse Observations with LAPIS-SHRED
summary: Reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of landslide runout from limited observations is a central challenge in geohazard assessment: transient flow dynamics are rarely observed directly, and available data are often confined to post-event deposits or brief monitoring windows. We apply LAPIS-SHRED (LAtent Phase Inference from Short time sequence using SHallow REcurrent Decoders) to reconstruct runout events near Mount St. Helens, USA. Trained on physics-based simulation ensembles, the framework supports both backward reconstruction from single frame and forward prediction from short initial window across different runout regimes. Using 32 sensor observations from a single timepoint, LAPIS-SHRED recovers complete runout trajectories with NRMSE below 5.8%, robust across varying observational and training conditions. Validation against observed deposits yields spatial correlation of r = 0.843 against the calibrated simulator's r = 0.853. These results suggest that latent-space temporal inference offers a viable pathway for spatiotemporal landslide reconstruction under extreme observational constraints typical of field settings.

title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. We propose MAPES, a multi-value alignment paradigm in which conflict resolution is a first-class concern at every pipeline stage: it first decomposes supervision into value-specific experts trained in isolated parameter subspaces, then recomposes them via preference-aware value merging and a lightweight harmonization stage that aligns the merged model with the expert ensemble. Across five preference alignment benchmarks, MAPES outperforms strong direct preference optimization (DPO) variants and multi-objective baselines on the benchmark-level average, with no large degradation on GSM8K and GPQA; matched controls isolate the contribution of each stage.

title: Crafting the Difference, Grounding the Evidence: Discriminative Concept Learning for Zero-Shot Skeleton Action Recognition
summary: LLM-generated descriptions enrich zero-shot skeleton-based action recognition but repeat cues shared by confusable actions. Their contextual semantics also lack explicit links to skeleton features. To address these challenges, we propose CRAFT, which couples Concept Refinement and Feature-grounded Tokens. Hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring identify concepts that distinguish each action from its closest rivals. Unique-QDPP selects complementary descriptions within each semantic slot and prevents their reuse across slots. This bank supervises learnable concept tokens that read motion and context cues from each skeleton. On fixed NTU-60 and NTU-120 splits, CRAFT improves five baselines spanning four recognition paradigms. ZSL accuracy and GZSL harmonic mean increase on every baseline-split pair, by 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on average. Random-split experiments extend these gains to three datasets, including PKU-MMD. Code will be released after acceptance.

title: TrajRealm: A Large-Scale Point Tracking Dataset with Diverse Dynamics
summary: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

title: Cross-Platform Production Signatures of State-Linked Information Operations
summary: An information operation active on several platforms presents different names, personas, and topics on each. Its working routine is harder to change. We call this routine the operation's production signature: the regularities in when and how its accounts post, reply, and repost. We measure it from timestamps and coarse action types only, using no content, profile metadata, or network ties, as timing and action profiles for accounts and learned action-gap policies for populations. We then ask which parts of a signature carry over to another platform and which belong to a single operation. We train models on Twitter archives of four state-linked operations and apply them to Internet Research Agency (IRA) accounts on Reddit, with no Reddit training labels. They rank the IRA accounts at AUC 0.90-0.94. Content detectors on the same route fall from 0.98 within a platform to 0.81. Daily phase accounts for most of the transfer. Posting volume reverses direction between platforms, and action mix follows the role accounts hold on each platform. What transfers is not unique to the IRA: a second operation shares the same working-hours window, and action-gap policies separate every operation from organic accounts (AUC 0.96-1.0) without consistently ranking their own operation first. On 938 Telegram channels, groups that forward the same sources keep ordinary hours and pace but publish original posts in the same ten-minute windows more often than chance. This pattern is invisible when accounts are examined one at a time. Our results suggest that timing and action traces learned on one platform can help flag likely operations on another.

title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
comment: 57 pages (30 main text, 27 supplementary material), 4 figures
summary: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $δ$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($δ$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($δ$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $δ$ = 1 minus $δ$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.

title: Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsibilities, we define role integrity as the preservation of an agent's functional responsibilities when it acts on its subordinates' material. To measure it, we introduce RI-Bench, a behavioral benchmark grounded in the structures and public records of three institutional hierarchies: peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry. We choose these hierarchies because their rules explicitly assign the senior role a duty toward subordinate material, and together they cover three basic duties: to weigh, to verify, and to relay. Rather than scoring output correctness, we measure how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material, using rule-based checks and a rubric-guided LLM judge calibrated against human annotation. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 agentic episodes, senior agents rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but often follow a majority of generic reviews (up to 71% of decisions) or drop witnesses' stated limitations (up to 65% of cited claims). Obligation prompts reduce these failures without removing them, and they also shift behavior in the control conditions. These findings motivate direct, obligation-specific evaluation of role integrity rather than inferring it from general capability or explicit role instructions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jxtse/ri-bench.

title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
summary: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.

title: How Does SAM-3 Adapt? Capacity, Update Geometry, and Domain Transfer
summary: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. Across these datasets, compact parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods often match or approach Full Fine-Tuning in DSC and IoU, suggesting that strong in-domain adaptation does not always require updating the full model. However, this performance cannot be explained by nominal adapter rank or trainable parameter count alone. To investigate why different methods perform similarly, we analyze their update spectra and their behavior under LoveDA Urban/Rural transfer. Our SVD analysis shows that Full Fine-Tuning updates are spectrally compressible. However, successful PEFT methods do not simply recover the same update directions; instead, they often concentrate changes in different components and subspaces. The domain-transfer study further shows that methods with similar in-domain performance can respond differently under distribution shift. Together, these results suggest that SAM-3 adaptation is often capacity-saturated in practice, while competitive fine-tuning arises through method-specific update paths rather than a single low-rank approximation to Full Fine-Tuning.

title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. We will release the appendix and code with a future version of this preprint
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.

title: Simulation-Based Testing of RCM-Constrained Robotic Software via Task Manifolds
summary: System-level testing of surgical robots requires generating executable test scenarios that exercise diverse, safety-critical behaviors. However, remote-center-of-motion (RCM) surgical manipulators operate within tightly constrained workspaces governed by coupled task geometry, inverse kinematics, and motor limits. Direct sampling in motor-command or Cartesian spaces frequently wastes testing budgets on physically unfeasible configurations. To address this limitation, we present a manifold-centered testing framework that decouples feasible test-domain construction from downstream test-generation strategies. Candidate inputs are generated directly within this constructed feasible domain and mapped to lower-level joint commands for simulation execution. Offline trajectory safety oracles and a spatial reference grid then evaluate failure yield and coverage. We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies. Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage. Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics. Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.

title: Improved (Minimum) Spanning Tree Construction in the HYBRID Model
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Full version of a paper to appear at OPODIS 2026
summary: In the HYBRID$_0$ model, vertices exchange $O(\log n)$-bit messages in synchronous rounds, both along input edges (local communication) and directly to vertices whose IDs they know (global communication). The local capacity is the maximum number of messages a vertex may send per round to each input neighbor, and the global capacity is the maximum number of global messages it may send, and also receive, per round. The standard capacity is local capacity $O(1)$ and global capacity $O(\log n)$. A well-formed tree (WFT) is a virtual tree of maximum degree $O(1)$ and diameter $O(\log n)$. Known algorithms construct a spanning tree (ST) and a WFT either in $O(\log n)$ rounds with global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$ or with standard capacity in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds. We give a randomized algorithm that constructs an ST and a WFT in every connected component of any graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability under standard capacity. Our approach is based on a $Δ$-pseudo-spanning representation ($Δ$-PSR): a virtual network of maximum degree $Δ$ with restoration information, such that any spanning tree of this network can be restored to a spanning tree of the input graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds. The algorithm of Götte et al. can be viewed as constructing an $O(\log n)$-PSR, which accounts for its global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$. Our main contribution is to construct an $O(1)$-PSR in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity. As applications, for $k$ distinct edge weights and any integer $1\le p\le k$, we construct an exact minimum spanning tree in $O((k/p)\log n)$ rounds with local capacity $O(p)$ and global capacity $O(p\log n)$, and the same tradeoff applies to $(1+ε)$-approximate minimum spanning trees. We also compute biconnected components, articulation points, and bridges in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity, down from the previous global capacity $O(\log^5 n)$.

title: Structure Over Scale: Rethinking Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is often framed as a choice between the expressivity of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and the efficiency of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We find that this framing misses an important variable: the geometry of the update. Under a common cold-start GRPO protocol, LoRA exhibits rank collapse: performance remains broadly stable at low rank, then fails abruptly as rank increases. On DeepMath-Hard, for example, accuracy drops from 73.1% at r=64 to 4.7% at r=128. In contrast, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) and Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation (QuanTA) remain stable over a wider tested optimization region and are competitive with FFT while updating less than 0.6% of the model parameters. Spectral analysis reveals a corresponding difference in learned update structure: collapsed LoRA concentrates its update energy into relatively few effective directions, whereas structured adapters produce substantially more distributed updates. These results suggest that nominal rank and parameter count alone are insufficient to characterize adaptation in RLVR - the structure imposed on the reachable update manifold also matters. Finally, across three 8B base models, adapter behavior aligns with both frozen-weight spectral structure and reported pre-training scale, motivating the Model Maturity Hypothesis: the adaptation geometry that works best may depend on properties already encoded during pre-training. We present this as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than a causal conclusion. The code can be found here https://github.com/Shrimpstanot/structure-over-scale

title: Where Structure Enters a World Model: From Predictive Fit to Physical Rollout
summary: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.

title: Git History Is a Pangenome: Repetition in Code Training Corpora and What Deduplication Removes, Keeps and Misses
summary: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.

title: The Vulnerability Window: Decision Instability in Quantized Reward Models
summary: Reward models and LLM judges are routinely quantized to 4 bits so that scoring many candidates stays affordable, and the usual check is that benchmark accuracy barely moves. That check is close to blind. Across eight reward models from two families (0.6B-8B), three generative judges and four 4-bit quantizers, quantization rewrites 1.1-12.3% of pairwise preference decisions on RewardBench while aggregate accuracy moves by as little as 0.03 points (p = 1.00), because the errors it fixes and introduces cancel. Flips concentrate where the full-precision margin is small relative to the quantization noise scale sigma: a Gaussian approximation Phi(-|m|/sigma) describes the aggregate rate, over-predicting it in all 30 scalar settings and failing for generative judges, and occupancy of the resulting vulnerability window falls from 25% to 7% with model size, which is what makes small judges fragile. The churn stays within noise under benign best-of-16 and becomes clear under adversarial pressure for some quantizers (146:54 harmful:helpful flips on one family, reversing sign on another). Downstream it changes what ships: across six (model, quantizer) pairs from two families, 14.6-65.7% of problems get a different best-of-64 selection while only 2.6-9.6% get a different final answer, with selections changing 5-8x more often than answers in every pair, and the pair the benchmark calls identical (0.03 points, p = 1.00) still changes 34.5% of them. Benchmark churn ranks that downstream change (rho = 0.89); benchmark accuracy does not order it reliably. Held-out audits then locate the useful diagnostic in the margin rather than the Gaussian: every margin-based predictor orders flips identically (AUC 0.927), and on the level a directly measured churn rate wins in-distribution. As a routing signal it is matched by plain top-k. The contribution is the characterization, not the model.

title: Co-Evolving Behavioral Agents and Detectors for Adaptive Information Operations
summary: Detectors of state-sponsored information operations (IOs) are trained on campaigns that platforms have already taken down. They lose much of their accuracy on an actor they have not seen, even though no operator in the archived data is trying to avoid them. A real operator wants two things, to reach an audience and to avoid being caught. We present IO-AI, a framework that gives simulated agents these two capabilities, engagement and evasion, and tests what each one does to detection. The agents are built from the posting behavior of real campaigns and choose the emotion, type, and timing of each post. An agent and a detector then train against each other in turn. We rank the trained agents by how hard they are to detect and train one detector on them from easiest to hardest. On 20 Twitter IO campaigns, this detector reduces missed detections of adaptive agents by 65% relative to a detector trained only on the archived campaigns, at a similar false-alarm rate. On actors it has never seen it reaches an F1 of 0.81, against 0.62. We find that an agent trained to seek engagement becomes easier to catch, because it learns the fast, emotional retweeting that archived campaigns were caught producing. An agent that was trained for engagement before the game keeps its engagement lead after it learns to evade. We also introduce a behavioral distance metric that compares two groups of accounts using only their unlabeled posting histories. The larger the distance between two groups, the worse a detector trained on one does on the other (Spearman rho = -0.58), so the metric can be used to choose which new groups to test first.

title: A Higher-Order Algorithm for Solving Time-Fractional Differential Equations via Rational Approximation of z^α as a Herglotz-Nevanlinna function
summary: Time-Fractional derivatives (TFDs) have been widely used in mathematical modeling of physical phenomena such as anomalous diffusion and memory effects of materials. Traditionally, TFD is handled {either by a direct method which saves almost all the memory and hence computationally expensive or a sum of exponential method (SOE) which decomposes the time domain improper integral into a local term and a history term} {approximated by} a sum of exponential functions. The limitation of the SOE approach is that{ the approximation error of the local term might result in large errors if the unknown function is not smooth enough at $0$ and can lead to over-dissipation of energy.} In this paper, we take a different approach and will focus on the Caputo derivative because the Caputo time derivative of a constant function is 0. We present a simple time-stepping algorithm based on the theory of Stieltjes-Markov functions, a subclass of the Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions. The key is in identifying the Stieltjes-Markov function structure hidden in the Laplace transform of the kernel function. Compared to most of the current methods in literature, the novelty of the results in this paper is manifold. First, no decomposition of integral is needed and our resulting approximation in the time domain contains a Dirac measure with carefully calculated strength, leading to a drastic decrease in the number of exponential functions needed in the approximation. Secondly, the choice of our interpolation points is based on the Mellin's inversion theorem and hence the interpolation error in the transformed domain is explicitly and rigorously linked to the error in the time-domain. {Finally, the resulting system is almost diagonal and hence can be easily sped up by using the Schur complement method.}

title: From Acting to Learning: Experience Selection toward Continually Learning Agents
summary: Successful agent interactions provide training data, but success alone does not determine which records a student should learn from. We examine experience selection for a 4B language agent as a component of continual agent learning. Nine selectors are compared across two fixed experience pools, eight initialization seeds, and two sampling seeds, yielding 288 trained students. Each student is evaluated on 128 development task groups with a common executor. With equal global selection freedom, 256 distinct contents, and 768 training presentations, optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45\% and 73.19\% success in the two pools. Its gains over global random selection are 8.25 and 5.96 percentage points; gains over global high-NLL selection are 4.10 and 4.05 points. All eight initialization-level contrasts are positive against both baselines in each pool. Relaxing coverage constraints improves gradient selection but reduces random-selection performance, showing that the ranking rule and selection space must be considered together. A separately frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups is complete; its equal-source gradient-minus-random and gradient-minus-high-NLL differences are +7.03 and +5.03 points, respectively.

title: Balanced Divide and Conquer for Rooted Maximum Agreement Forests
summary: We develop a balanced divide-and-conquer framework for the maximum agreement forest problem on rooted binary phylogenetic tree--forest instances. The goal is a common subforest with the fewest components; budget $k$ bounds the increase relative to the input forest. We balance edges associated with an unknown optimum to obtain three subproblems with smaller budgets. Branching separates the inputs, while temporary marker leaves allow a global optimum to be recovered from independently computed optimal solutions. For any fixed $B>\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$, the framework converts a tree--forest solver running in $O^*(B^k)$ time into one running in $O^*((\sqrt{\varphi B})^k)$ time. Starting from an $O^*(2.3391^k)$-time solver, two applications yield an $O^*(1.7743^{k^*})$-time fixed-parameter algorithm for two trees, where $k^*$ is the number of components in a maximum agreement forest minus one. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a fixed number of applications yields $O^*((\varphi+\varepsilon)^{k^*})$ time. Here $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors, whose degree and constants may depend on $\varepsilon$.

title: Real-Anchored Complementary Evidence for Generalizable AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: Evolving generative models challenge detector generalization, as methods trained on generated examples may rely on generator-specific cues. By contrast, authentic photographs share regularities rooted in physical image formation and acquisition, providing a common reference beyond individual generators. Building on these regularities, we propose Real-Anchored Complementary Evidence (RACE), which learns complementary global and local detection evidence using only authentic training images. First, the global pathway combines frozen and learned representations to assess proximity to authentic references. Next, it incorporates responses to controlled perturbations, complementing static compatibility with representation sensitivity. The local pathway then reconstructs complete trace descriptors, using intermediate features and signed perturbation responses as context while restricting detection evidence to static terminal-residual reconstruction errors. Finally, authentic-image statistics align the global and local scores for fusion, and an independent authentic set calibrates a decision threshold held fixed across test generators. Across six benchmarks, RACE achieves the highest average AUROC of 96.59% among the compared methods, reaching 97.18% on five out-of-domain benchmarks. Together with robustness to image perturbations and variation in authentic-image sources, these results support authentic-image regularities as a transferable basis for detection across diverse generators and image conditions.

title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
summary: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$α$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$α$-C$α$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$α$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20° of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$α$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.

title: PhysForce: Physics-aware Force Control for Interactive Video World Model
summary: Interactive video world models aim to predict how visual environments evolve in response to user interventions, including physically consistent state changes induced by applied forces. Existing methods often represent forces as motion trajectories, which may introduce inappropriate motion priors, causing the model to over-rely on encoded displacement patterns. More fundamentally, the model's internal representations do not reliably localize force-induced state changes, making it difficult to associate applied forces with their resulting physical responses. Also, limited force-annotated data make it difficult to produce physically consistent and temporally stable predictions in unseen scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PhysForce, a two-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning through three complementary components. During supervised fine-tuning, (1) the Latent Force Intervention Encoder maps force location, direction, and magnitude into the video latent space without exposing future motion; and (2) the Physics Attribution Network associates force interventions with localized changes in the latent state, strengthening the learning of physical responses to applied forces. During reinforcement learning, (3) Physics-Aware Reinforcement Learning uses self-supervised rewards on out-of-distribution videos to improve physical consistency and generalization. Extensive experiments show that PhysForce improves force responsiveness, physical consistency, and generalization, demonstrating its effectiveness for interactive video world models.

title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.

title: BusemannFormer: Horospherical Self-Attention for Hyperbolic Graph Transformers
summary: Hyperbolic neural networks excel on hierarchical graph data, yet existing hyperbolic Transformers largely adapt conventional attention without explicitly exploiting the ideal boundary, a geometric structure closely tied to tree hierarchy. We propose Horospherical Self-Attention (HSA): each query selects an ideal-boundary direction and scores keys by their Busemann depth along that direction, yielding a token-to-token hyperbolic attention kernel. We establish a flat-limit connection to dot-product attention, characterize score level sets as horospheres, and bound key-side gradients. HSA is integrated into BusemannFormer, a fully hyperbolic graph Transformer, with a log-depth variant that uses query depth to modulate attention concentration. We further introduce a finite-boundary-dictionary extension supporting linear-complexity global attention. Experiments on hierarchical and citation graphs show that BusemannFormer-LD outperforms the evaluated baselines on several node-classification benchmarks and achieves competitive performance across diverse graph structures.

title: FedQCal: Quadratic Programming with Dual-Space Calibration for One-Shot Federated Learning
summary: One-shot federated learning must combine heterogeneous client models after a single upload. Different local class distributions make it difficult to decide which client updates to retain. We propose FedQCal, which uses a reference model trained on a small labeled server set to define alignment requirements for aggregation. The key idea is to retain sufficient reference alignment while avoiding unnecessarily large aggregation coefficients. A minimum-norm quadratic program (QP) enforces these requirements. Classification loss on the same server examples selects a merge through two dual variables, so the alignment thresholds need not be prescribed in advance. We prove that the selected coefficients remain exact QP solutions at their induced thresholds. A perturbation bound explains how coefficient norm limits the amplification of projection errors. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN show gains over one-round FedAvg in most settings. Ablations support reference-guided weighting and coefficient calibration, even with one labeled server image per class.

title: Learning from Incomplete Actions: Interval Motion Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Visual labeling of egocentric demonstrations often leaves contiguous gaps in action supervision. Reliable poses around a gap still provide its net translation and rotation. We use this information to train vision-language-action policies while preserving ordinary flow matching on reliable local actions. A composition objective constrains the aggregate motion of missing-action estimates, combining multiple fixed windows when a gap exceeds the policy horizon. A shared interval branch learns from reliable endpoints and supplies the composition target. On LIBERO with 20% of demonstrations and 70.5% missing actions, the main method achieves 87.9% mean success over three training runs. In one paired comparison with matched observation exposure and training cost, its advantage over masking is 10.5%. On Ego-informed RoboTwin gaps, success is 45.4%, versus 40.3% for masking. On five real-robot tasks, mean success is 59.6%, versus 54.8% for interval flow matching alone and 48.8% for masking.

title: PACE-WM: Parallel World Modeling with Action History for Visual Planning
summary: JEPA-style world models support visual planning by predicting future representations conditioned on future actions. However, similar observations can conceal different motion states, making temporal context essential for interpreting future action effects. We propose PACE-WM, a parallel world model that uses executed-action history to contextualize future prediction and planning. Specifically, PACE-WM maintains a recurrent memory of executed actions and uses this memory to condition a causal Transformer. PACE-WM predicts multiple future representations in parallel without recursive predicted-state feedback within each prediction window. We further introduce Reference-Anchored Minimum Progress (RAMP) for action selection during planning. RAMP scores candidate actions by their predicted goal improvement along direct and split paths relative to a shared reference. Across four visual planning tasks, PACE-WM with RAMP achieves an average success rate of $98\%$ and plans approximately $7$-$9\times$ faster than autoregressive LeWM under matched CEM settings. We also construct four controlled benchmarks to evaluate PACE-WM's capabilities in motion disambiguation, goal-relative motion, and goal adaptation. Project page is available at https://github.com/LHS180/PACE-WM.

title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search
summary: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.

title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations.
